claims.text: The tuned SQLite compile-flag set (with prepare_v3) is accepted; per-call savings are individually too small to measure but stack with isLeaf bindings.
SQLITE_ENABLE_BATCH_ATOMIC_WRITE is a zero-risk compile flag: it activates via VFS capability detection (Android F2FS) with no effect elsewhere and no API change.

Remembering a SQL's last row count and pre-sizing `decodeQuery`'s result buffer from it is not worth the two-field cache entry: list growth is already cheap (only ~3-4 doublings even for a 10k-row read) and the measurable improvement sits below the release-suite noise floor.
claims.conditions: release suite, 3 repeats vs baseline, 2 wins / 0 regressions / 61 neutral · 2026-04 · backfilled 2026-08

claims.text: `decodeQuery`'s initial `List<Object?>.filled(colCount * 256, null)` must not be shrunk. Cutting it to `colCount * 4` regressed every many-small-query workload (Stream Churn +44%, Batched Write Inside Transaction +40%), because the VM's null-fill fast path makes one large pre-sized allocation cheaper per slot than a small one that then has to grow.
claims.conditions: release suite, 0 wins / 4 regressions / 59 neutral · 2026-04 · backfilled 2026-08

claims.text: Computing the selectIfChanged result hash in C during the step loop is a large win (-39%) on the re-query path with zero measurable regression; hash code consolidates to a single C implementation.
sqlite3mc version bumps should wait for safer point releases when the newest SQLite release is a fresh .0.
Byte-stream hash-loop changes need long-text stream workloads before they are meaningfully testable.
Top-level transaction control had removable SQLite prepare/finalize work; cached control statements remove it.
The archived 8-byte FNV byte fold is a clear win once the workload carries 4KB TEXT cells; the long-text unchanged-fanout benchmark was the blocker to seeing it.
Savepoint string-allocation cost is below the decision threshold even at 50 SAVEPOINTs per iteration — per-isolate-round-trip cost dominates nested transaction control.

Exp 119's 3,590-park signal was upstream over-dispatch from StreamEngine._flushQueue, not reader-pool admission; snapshotting availableWorkerCount once and decrementing per pop drops parking to zero. Future dispatch work needs a different counter.
A guarded ASCII fast path removes per-string UTF-8 allocation in wide batch parameter packing without changing the public API or weakening Unicode fallback.

Direct UTF-8 payload writing removes the same per-string allocation for non-ASCII batches (focused Unicode 10k x20 -13.5%, emoji -27.8%), with Dart-compatible surrogate handling private to the encoder.
Row-level dirty precision can remove the keyed-PK miss-path cost (intersection_entries 10000 -> 3; writer-burst wall 25.54 -> 12.45 ms) — rejected as shipped complexity, preserved as potential.
On A11c overlap the reader-worker port handler is the largest remaining reachable main-isolate slice (28.57% of burst+drain wall); subscriber-fanout emit is <1% and is not the optimization target.
Pinned Tracelite profile runs produce decision-useful structured evidence: point queries are median dispatch-bound, merge rounds are work-bound, and allocation/RSS costs hide behind wall time alone.
The 3.53.0 default-FP-rounding hazard does not reach resqlite output (REAL values never go through sqlite3_column_text); the vendoring bump waits on a .2 point release per exp 090's policy.

SQLite-facing write calls are a minority of writer-side burst wall on active stream workloads (A11c 9.4%, keyed-PK 18.1%); residual writer/request wall is the largest bucket after subtracting SQLite and invalidation.

The Tracelite workload-summary explanation layer emits the interpretation exp 143 had to recover manually, and validates stable insight IDs so a thin artifact fails loudly instead of looking complete.
The 8-byte FNV fold scales acceptably to mixed 32KB TEXT+BLOB long payloads (3.446 ms median beside 2.356 ms for 4KB TEXT), and the streaming suite now covers that shape.
At 32KB cells on a pool-of-4 fleet the byte-stream fold is no longer the dominant wall component; unrolling beyond the 8-byte FNV body is below noise. Hash-loop unrolling on this shape is closed.
selectBytes sends a Uint8List view over the reader's native json_buf and never sacrifices; the single send copy is the floor for this path.

Phase-ordered A/B gates confound code deltas with time-correlated drift; cvPct + classifyDriftFlag encode the CV-asymmetry and order-flip sign-reversal signatures so every A/B no longer re-derives them by hand.
A chartable experiment with no linked benchmark run and no Benchmark Run opt-out silently drops off the chart; the linker now errors, closing the gap that left ~18 experiments unmapped.
Removing reader-pool parallelism (one-reader runtime, 64x64KB payloads) still shows no 16-byte FNV win over the 8-byte fold; the single-stream candidate from exp 173 is consumed.

selectBytes' bounded RSS high-water becomes pathological under concurrent large bursts (8 x 8MB pins 32MB for the connection's life); the 1MB-cap + 256KB last-len reclaim makes the policy safe, and readerJsonBufHighWaterBytes makes it observable.

The single-row direct-ASCII allocateParams rewrite is materially beneficial once bound text crosses mid-tens-of-KB (-15% at 16KB to -32% at larger sizes); encoder isolation separates the mechanism question from workload materiality.
Direct UTF-8 packing for single-row non-ASCII params removes one temp allocation plus one copy per string; CJK rows improve ~31-39% from 16KB through 1MB.
Savepoint naming compression moves best-case control rows but the representative nested-write fanout does not reproduce across the order flip — rejected on the load-bearing row.
Lazy nested-savepoint materialization only helps empty nested bodies; fusing SAVEPOINT + first execute regresses the meaningful nested-write shape in both pass orders.

The per-execute round-trip floor inside db.transaction() is mechanically removable for Future.wait bursts, but the pattern has no idiomatic case in the public API — bulk atomic writes belong on executeBatch. Rejected on pattern, not numbers.

native/resqlite.c is no longer ISA-agnostic-scalar-only: a NEON vqtbl4q_u8 base64 kernel (~2x on 4KB payloads) ships behind an __aarch64__ gate with the scalar 12-bit-LUT encoder as fallback. Keep SIMD kernels noinline so the small-input scalar path's code gen is untouched.

A mutable Uint8List param is the one write value SendPort.send truly copies; wrapping params >= 256 KB in TransferableTypedData lands that one copy in external memory instead of on the GC heap (~15-20% on 256-512 KB single-row inserts).

json_write_string's SWAR escape scan re-enters the 8-byte fast skip after each dirty chunk instead of abandoning it on the first escapable byte, so a sparse escape downgrades only the chunk containing it rather than the whole tail. Realistic multi-line TEXT encodes 23% faster (256B, newline every ~80B) and the one-early-escape extreme 45%; the escape-free path is byte-identical and measures parity. Cost is +6.0% on pathological dense-escape 256B (~1/3 escapable bytes), one extra SWAR probe per all-dirty chunk.
claims.conditions: Apple Silicon · AOT · focused order-flipped A/B (5 BASE / 4 CAND medians) · 2026-07

claims.text: A fast-scan's abandon-on-first-miss structure is invisible to all-safe and all-dirty test shapes and only costs on the sparse-miss middle, which is the common real distribution. The pre-235 harness held dense-escape and late-escape lanes and neither exercised it; the regression pocket appeared only once sparse-newline and sparse-early lanes existed.
claims.conditions: harness-design finding · generalises beyond the TEXT escaper

claims.text: Blob result cells >= 256 KB decode straight into TransferableTypedData (native->external, one copy) and cross by ownership move; main-isolate receive boundaries materialize them back to Uint8List views. Blob-heavy reads 3-6x faster; tx.select ~6-7x.
The sacrifice decision weighs estimatedBytes - transferableBytes so TTD-wrapped cells do not force a sacrifice.

Exp 234's blob-transfer win does not extend to executeBatch: wrapping per-set blobs is a reproduced regression. The mechanism is many independent write round-trips parking fresh blobs on the young heap — one batch round-trip does not have it.

Batching only already-parked plain selects in pool-sharded envelopes (capped at four) improves 20 point reads ~-26/-33% without a new public API; sharding avoids exp 209's one-worker large-read collapse. Rejected as shipped complexity, preserved as potential.

Sacrifice is a state-changing treatment (kills a worker, respawns, clears caches): it cannot be A/B'd in place inside one live pool. Send-vs-exit decomposes into distinct estimands — intrinsic transfer, pool capacity, decode — that must be measured separately.
A TransferableTypedData wrap helps iff the payload's default SendPort destination is the GC heap; a native-backed view gains nothing — the wrap relocates the one copy and adds machinery.

Blob-param wrapping is identity-keyed (one wrapper per unique buffer, referenced at every position, materialized once per envelope), so caller aliasing survives the hop instead of exploding into N external copies (~27x at N=32 under per-occurrence wrapping).

Sacrifice opens no pool-capacity hole at the production pool size: the no-sacrifice lane had the highest parked queue-wait (~+19%), because send's copy blocks the worker longer than Isolate.exit plus an overlapped respawn. Eager respawn measured inert.
SendPort.send's cost tracks the mutable flat-list slot count, not payload bytes: strings and numbers are shared by reference (a 400 KB string adds ~0 us), while the values array is copied per slot.
Isolate.exit is zero-copy with a ~47 us fixed premium; its sendability walk also scales with slots, just more gently than send's copy. Intrinsic crossover ~48k slots.

The sacrifice trigger routes on mutable slot count (values.length > 32k, the all-integer equivalent of 256 KB); the byte accounting is deleted. Bytes for mutable payloads, slots for structure. Big-TEXT misroute fixed: 131->91 us, 1.00->0.00 sacrifices/select.

Exp 233's checkpoint storm was a trigger-policy failure, not inherent to off-writer PASSIVE work: observed-reset/high-water re-arming fixes the storm and first threshold-crossing p50 improves ~53-64%. Rejected for now, mechanism preserved.

Across five AOT process runs, a direct-handle step-only reference found no universal dominant worker-path bucket: estimated decode/result construction was 49%, 63%, 40%, and 51% of full query/decode wall for 10k x 20 INTEGER, 10k mixed, 5k x 4 INTEGER, and 5k TEXT shapes. The full worker-path proxy was typically 91%, 92%, 84%, and 94% of separately measured main-observed Database.select() latency.
claims.conditions: Apple M-series · arm64 macOS · Dart 3.12.2 · AOT CLI native-asset bundle · five fresh processes · 2026-08

claims.text: The post-transfer large-read residual is shape-dependent rather than a single Dart-decode bottleneck, so it does not justify a broad ResultSet storage rewrite; a future candidate must first establish a workload-specific eligible phase against public select() wall.
claims.conditions: INTEGER, mixed INTEGER/TEXT, and long-TEXT result shapes · AOT · 2026-08

claims.text: A stream always resolves to an emission or an error, never silence. When a write dirties an entry mid-initial-query the comparison baseline is poisoned so the catch-up re-query is guaranteed to emit, and that emission is the stream's first. Suppressing the initial emission while leaving the baseline set to the rows it replaced is what stranded streams permanently silent.
claims.conditions: M1 Pro · deterministic regression test (40k-row seed) · 2026-07

claims.text: An intermittent test failure reproducing at ~1-in-3 is a bug, not a flake. This one was dismissed three times in one session, partly because the test's own comment asserted the shape could not flake — a false confidence marker actively redirects investigation, and reading the actual failure text ('emitted x Stream closed') would have identified the mechanism immediately.

Clearing a stream's comparison baseline must clear the row count, not the hash: selectIfChanged requires both to match, and an empty result legitimately hashes to 0, so a hash sentinel of 0 is reachable rather than impossible and would leave empty-result streams silent. The row count is nullable end to end, with null meaning 'no baseline' — which also retired a pre-existing magic -1 in the request type.
claims.conditions: review finding · guarded by the empty-result regression test · 2026-07

claims.text: A stream never emits rows it already knows a write superseded: when the initial query is dirtied mid-flight the comparison baseline is poisoned and only the corrected result is emitted. This costs ~0.4-1.4 ms of time-to-correct-value and removes the stale frame that emit-then-correct rendered on every raced stream; unraced streams are unaffected.
claims.conditions: M1 Pro · 1k/20k/60k seed race windows · 12 samples/shape · 2026-07

claims.text: A one-call native interpreter that preserves independent autocommits does not clear the writer-burst bar: homogeneous inserts improved 17.7% then only 3.6% across the order flip, while integer-only no-op updates regressed 17.7% and 13.9%.

Storing numeric result columns as typed arrays (Int64List/Float64List) instead of boxing into a flat List<Object?> makes worker-side result build 60-90% faster (largest on REAL: doubles always box, ~10x on 10k x 20 REAL). This win is worker wall, off the main isolate.
claims.conditions: M-series · AOT · worker->main SendPort A/B · two order-flipped passes · 2026-07

claims.text: A columnar container's transfer win (73-91% cheaper hop vs the boxed flat list) does not move production's main-isolate metric: results large enough for transfer to matter (>32768 structural slots) already zero-copy via Isolate.exit, and sub-threshold results save only tens of microseconds, below the select() round-trip floor. The broad columnar rewrite is therefore rejected.

The one real primary-metric signal from columnar storage is main-isolate integer consume ~2x faster (Int64List sequential access, no covariant-load barrier, vs pointer-chasing a List<Object?> of Smis), reproduced -48 to -52% on every integer lane in both orders. REAL consume is only neutral (box-on-access nearly cancels the locality gain) and columnar never regresses consume, refuting exp 081's box-on-access fear for the columnar (not binary-slab) shape.
claims.conditions: M-series · AOT · main-isolate full-scan as Object? · 2026-07

claims.text: Classifying a TEXT cell as pure ASCII in resqlite_step_row (branch-free SWAR, memcpy-based unaligned loads) instead of in fastDecodeText removes one ExternalTypedData allocation and one bounds-checked Dart scan per cell, worth a reproduced -12.3% / -10.4% on 10k x 8 short-ASCII select(), -14.3% / -10.7% at 40 B, -22.2% / -19.4% at 400 B, and -24.4% / -19.2% on the repo's canonical 6-column mixed row (id INTEGER + 4 TEXT + REAL, from benchmark/shared/seeder.dart). The mixed lane's p50 is its signal; its p90 is noisy across passes and is not a tail regression.
claims.conditions: M1 Pro · AOT CLI bundle · cross-worktree A/B · two order-flipped passes · 31 samples/lane · 2026-08

claims.text: The isolated per-cell mechanism is 6-15 ns, or 12-49% of fastDecodeText's wall depending on payload width (6-14 B: -12% / -34%; 20-40 B: -36% / -39%; 200 B: -49% / -48%). At 80k TEXT cells per lane that is 0.5-1.2 ms, matching the end-to-end deltas in order of magnitude.
claims.conditions: M1 Pro · AOT microbenchmark over malloc'd 8-aligned ASCII payloads · 2026-08

claims.text: An accumulate-then-test SWAR scan that always walks the whole value is not a regression for non-ASCII TEXT. Ordinary CJK text measured -2.4% / -1.7%, and the shape built to expose the trade — a 400 B value with its one multibyte character at byte 0, so the native scan walks the whole payload to learn what the old Dart scan settled in its first word — measured +1.1% / -1.0%. That lane runs ~4.9 ms against ~0.7 ms for the same payload in ASCII: utf8.decode over the value dwarfs a SWAR pass over it, so the 'wasted' scan is an order of magnitude cheaper than the decode it precedes.
claims.conditions: M1 Pro · AOT · 10k x 8 CJK TEXT (~36 B/cell) and 2k x 4 400 B early-nonascii · two order-flipped passes · 2026-08

claims.text: A cross-worktree focused A/B carrying a lane whose code is byte-identical in both arms reads the per-binary layout offset directly. Exp 259's INTEGER-only control moved +0.2% / -2.9% — opposite signs, inside the 3% effect floor — which is what licenses trusting the text lanes without falling back to exp 254's single-binary runtime toggle.

Sizing `decodeQuery`'s result buffer from a main-isolate memory of what the same SQL returned before — applied at the first growth, never to the initial allocation — is worth a reproduced -25.1% / -24.8% on 10k x 20 INTEGER, -32.2% / -33.7% on 5k x 4 INTEGER, and -33.6% / -32.3% on the repo's canonical 6-column product row at 10k rows (3.5 ms -> 2.3 ms), measured end to end through the public `select()`. Both controls (200-row and point reads, which never reach the growth path) move opposite signs inside the 3% floor, and both mispredict guards are neutral.
claims.conditions: M1 Pro · AOT CLI bundle · cross-worktree A/B · two order-flipped passes · 31 samples/lane · 2026-08

claims.text: Buffer growth, not cell decoding, is most of the Dart-side cost of a large read. Reproducing the decode loop over a fixed cell buffer at 10k x 20 INTEGER: doubling from the 256-row initial allocation 2318 us, pre-sized 865 us, loads + switch with no list store 331 us, and `List.filled(200000, null)` alone 405 us. Exp 251's 2524 us for the same shape's `Dart result construction` is therefore a growth measurement more than a decode one.
claims.conditions: M1 Pro · AOT standalone microbenchmark · 40 reps · 2026-08

claims.text: A worker-local cache cannot hold anything learned from a large result. `Isolate.exit` on a result over `sacrificeSlotThreshold` ends the worker, so a size hint kept in the per-worker schema cache won 30-35% on sub-threshold reads and ~1% on the 200k-slot lane; the same hint carried on the request from the main isolate won -25% there.
claims.conditions: M1 Pro · AOT · focused A/B, both hint placements against one baseline · 2026-08

claims.text: Pre-sizing from a converged row hint lowers total bytes allocated per query by 14-61% (the doubling sequence's intermediate arrays stop existing) but does NOT uniformly lower peak buffer capacity. Doubling's overshoot is 1x-2x depending on where the result falls relative to a power-of-two boundary; a converged hint's is always 1.25x. Peak capacity is 23.7% smaller for a result that overshoots a boundary (all three primary lanes) and 22-25% LARGER for one that lands just under it (mixed6-1k, and 2048 rows x 6 columns). Arithmetic on the allocation path only — no RSS or heap sampling was taken, so a workload sensitive to peak rather than churn needs its own measurement.
claims.conditions: derived from the growth path, not measured · 2026-08

claims.text: A focused-harness memory guard must gate on `ProcessInfo.maxRss` with one process per lane, not on a sampled `currentRss` peak. The two disagreed by 76 percentage points about the same change (sampled peak +75%, `maxRss` -1.7%) on a lane whose results cross `sacrificeSlotThreshold`, because sacrificed isolates return pages and make `currentRss` a retention signal rather than a high-water. Repeatability across five isolated runs per arm is <=0.6 MB, mechanically inert lanes read identical across arms, and sampling moves wall time 1.3-2.4%, inside the 3% floor.
claims.conditions: M1 Pro · AOT CLI bundle · one process per lane · 2026-08

claims.text: Exp 260 lowers peak RSS rather than raising it: `maxRss` falls -2.1% on 10k x 20 INTEGER, -11.5% on the canonical 6-column product row at 10k rows, and -28.0% on 5k x 4 INTEGER, with the point-read control flat at -0.3%. This supersedes the arithmetic in claim 260.4, which predicted peak capacity could rise 22-25% for results landing just under a doubling boundary.
claims.conditions: M1 Pro · AOT · maxRss, one process per lane, 21 samples · 2026-08

claims.text: Peak read-path memory was flat within ~1 MB from v0.3.0 (2026-05-03) to exp 259 (2026-08-03) across eight checkpoints and roughly forty merged experiments, including the whole transfer-shape arc, while wall time on the same runs fell 25-40%. The only movement in the window is exps 259 and 260, both downward. No memory regression has accumulated.
claims.conditions: M1 Pro · AOT · harness source held constant, rebuilt per checkpoint · maxRss, one process per lane · 2026-08

claims.text: `select()` holds far more than its payload: `mixed6-10k` reads a table containing roughly 1.5 MB of data and peaks at 95 MB, and 89.5 MB of the pre-exp-260 figure is resident before the measured reads begin. The ~60x ratio has never been decomposed, and exps 008/032's lazy and facade result shapes were assessed against wall time rather than against this.
claims.conditions: M1 Pro · AOT · maxRss and post-warmup resident, one process per lane · 2026-08

claims.text: Release-suite crash resilience must persist per scenario, not per repeat. A SIGKILL during scenario 10 of 16 preserves 9 scenarios and 153 resqlite metrics with `repeatCount: 0` and `partial: true`; the same kill produced no artifact before. Against the crash that actually occurs — the sqlite_async peer dying at scenario 15 — this preserves fourteen scenarios including every read, write and streaming lane.

The release suite can now fail on a memory regression. `compareMemory` returns wins/regressions/neutral plus the regressed benchmark names alongside the existing table, and `--fail-on-memory-regression` exits non-zero. Thresholds are unchanged (per-benchmark bootstrap MDE, 0.5 MB floor) — only the verdict is newly actionable. Opt-in rather than default: a local run reports without failing.

The Dart representation of a `select()` row costs 256 B/row for the canonical product row's five non-key columns — obtained by differencing the 6-column marginal (396 B/row) against the 1-column `id` marginal (140 B/row), since both projections make the same btree leaves resident and the shared term is storage-side rather than representational. That is 1.9x their 134.9 B of cell content, and 0.86x a first-principles accounting of what they must occupy (~296 B). Measured as a single live result, one process per lane, seeding held constant at 20,000 rows.
claims.conditions: M1 Pro · AOT CLI bundle · maxRss, one process per lane, single read held live · payload averaged over the full seeded range · 2026-08

claims.text: resqlite's resident floor before any row is read is 20.5 MB, of which 14.0 MB is a bare AOT Dart process; seeding 20,000 rows adds ~12 MB more, and a live 10,000-row result adds 3.6 MB. The result is the smallest term, so a payload-to-peak ratio taken on a read-and-discard workload is a statement about the floor.
claims.conditions: M1 Pro · AOT · maxRss, one process per lane · 2026-08

claims.text: `selectBytes` costs 676 B/row against `select`'s 396 B/row on the same rows. It avoids Dart object allocation, not bytes: JSON repeats every column name per row and quotes and escapes every value. Reach for it to reduce allocation churn, not footprint.
claims.conditions: M1 Pro · AOT · maxRss, one process per lane, single read held live · 2026-08

claims.text: A per-row cost of ~140 B/row is shared by every projection of the same table and is not part of the result representation: the 1-column `id` lane pays it as fully as the 6-column `select` lane, because a btree leaf holds the whole row regardless of what is projected. Its mechanism is bounded but not established — it scales with rows read, is indifferent to column count, and resqlite opens connections with mmap_size = 256 MB and cache_size = -8192, so mmap'd file pages becoming resident, WAL pages, and a cold reader page cache are all live candidates. Any future per-row memory figure must difference two projections or it charges this to the wrong layer.
claims.conditions: M1 Pro · AOT · maxRss, one process per lane · mechanism not discriminated · 2026-08

claims.text: Sizing `decodeQuery`'s *initial* result allocation from a main-isolate high-water mark of the rows a SQL has ever returned, clamped into 1..256 rows so it can only shrink below the fixed default, is worth a reproduced -13.5% on a 1-row 6-column point read and -27.1% on a 1-row 21-column one. Four alternating-order lane-isolated AOT passes, 61 samples each, on a host at 52-61% CPU idle with controls inside +/-1.7% (`int20-10k` +0.3%, `mixed6-10k` -0.4%). The win scales with projection width because what a one-row result wastes is `colCount * 255` slots. Every lane whose result outgrows the initial buffer is neutral by construction, not by measurement: it clamps to the same 256 rows both arms allocate.
claims.conditions: M1 Pro · AOT CLI bundle · lane-isolated, 4 alternating-order passes, 61 samples/lane · host 52-61% idle · 2026-08

claims.text: A result-buffer size hint whose failure mode is under-prediction must be a high-water mark, not a sliding window. Taking the larger of a SQL's last two row counts — the mirror of exp 260's smaller-of-two — cost +40% in all four order-flipped passes on a statement returning 3,300 rows behind bursts of eight 20-row executions, because the two observations preceding each large execution are both small, so the penalty repeats on every large read instead of once. Under a high-water mark the same lane is neutral (-1.3% mean) and the one-time cost of a statement's first jump from small to large is +1.6% (927.5 -> 942.5 us median over 50 fresh processes per arm), consistent with an arithmetic account of four extra growths, ~15,200 extra slot copies and ~13,800 extra slots zero-filled.
claims.conditions: M1 Pro · AOT · `undershoot-mid` lane, 3,300 rows behind 8x20-row poison · first-jump figure from --warmup=0 --samples=1, 50 processes/arm · 2026-08

claims.text: Exp 067's mechanism claim is per-slot true and decision-irrelevant. `List<Object?>.filled(n, null, growable: true)` followed by a write of `k` slots and a truncation to `k` costs 423 ns at n=1536/k=6 against 21.5 ns at n=12/k=6, and 1223 ns at n=5376/k=21 against 46.5 ns at n=42/k=21 — so the large allocation is roughly six times cheaper per slot and twenty times more expensive in total. Any Dart allocation claim of the form 'the VM's fast path makes the larger one cheaper' must be quoted per call, not per slot.
claims.conditions: M1 Pro · standalone AOT reproduction of the allocation shape, no FFI or SQLite · 20,000 calls/round, 200 rounds · 2026-08

claims.text: The release suite runs, and exp 262's per-scenario persistence now demonstrably preserves a killed run. The suite completes 14 of 16 scenarios — every read, write, streaming and app-shaped lane — and aborts inside the sqlite_async peer at `[15/16] Memory`, the pre-existing #282 crash, additionally wedging the parent rather than exiting. The killed run still wrote an artifact with 169 metrics, correctly self-marked `partial: true`, `scenariosCompleted: 14`, `repeatCount: 0`; exps 260 and 261 were killed inside repeat 1 before that mechanism existed and produced nothing. The artifact is single-sample and unpaired, so it is a no-regression sanity check (point query 160,798 qps, 1,000-row `select()` 0.349 ms, batch insert 1,000 rows 0.389 ms, invalidation 0.058 ms — all at or better than README's published figures) and not evidence for any candidate.
claims.conditions: M1 Pro · macOS 26.2 · Dart 3.12.2 · --repeat=5, killed in repeat 1 at scenario 15 · single-sample, no baseline · 2026-08

claims.text: Exp 264's own change to `ReaderPool._record` put exp 260's growth hint at risk, and the fix is capacity/priority rather than ordering. Removing exp 260's `rowCount <= initialResultRows` insert guard let every point read take one of the 32 `_rowHints` slots, so a statement that has proven large is evicted by point-read churn and loses its hint. Measured on the new `hint-thrash-overflows` lane (5,000 x 5 read behind 40 distinct one-off statements per sample): pre-264 597-631 us against exp-264 826-919 us, a systematic +40-46% in which the slower arm's fastest sample beat the faster arm's slowest. Least-recently-used promotion does NOT fix it (no improvement measured, and it costs the main isolate a map remove-and-reinsert per read); raising `_rowHintMax` to 128 does (620 us), and so does preferring an eviction victim whose `highWater <= initialResultRows` (565 us). The latter shipped, and a four-pass re-measurement on a quiet host confirms both halves: the lane runs -29.5% against the unfixed arm in all four passes and is level with pre-264 (-0.2%), so exp 260's reach is restored rather than merely improved, while the fix is inert on the hot path (both point lanes sign-flip, both controls +/-0.1%) exactly as its structure predicts -- `_evictionVictim` is unreachable until the memory overflows its 32 entries. Unfixed, the same lane is +41.6% against pre-264. Specifically: it restores exp 260's exclusive tenure without a magic capacity, costs nothing per read because the O(32) scan runs only on an overflowing miss, and is gated deterministically in `test/reader_pool_test.dart` rather than through the noisy lane.
claims.conditions: M1 Pro · AOT · `hint-thrash-overflows`, 4 alternating-order passes, 61 samples · host 52-61% idle · 2026-08

claims.text: Every wall-time figure in exp 264 was collected on a host at 0.0% CPU idle. `top` reported 57% user / 43% sys / 0% idle, with an unrelated Virtualization.framework VM at 190% CPU, FSEvents at 57%, and other Dart processes at 100% and 44%; load average read 33/39/50 on ten cores. Six `run_release.dart` processes from earlier sessions were also resident, wedged 1-4 days at 0.0% CPU — the #282 peer crash does not merely kill a run, it leaves the parent blocked forever, and they accumulate. The order-flipped design cancels a stationary component and the controls held to +/-2%, and the mechanism is independently corroborated by a standalone allocation probe with no isolates or SQLite (423 ns vs 21.5 ns per call) whose magnitudes match the lane deltas; the *direction and mechanism* are therefore sound. The precise percentages were not, and were re-measured once the host freed up: the narrow point read moved from -7.4% to -13.5% and the wide one from -27.4% to -27.1%, with controls tightening from +/-4% to +/-1.7%. So the saturation cost about six points of accuracy on the smaller effect and none on the larger. The general hazard stands: a per-read microsecond measurement on a saturated host is dominated by reader-isolate scheduling latency. A confirmation pass attempted late in the run read +50.6% on `int20-10k`, a lane the candidate cannot reach, which is how the saturation was discovered. The same host had 352-440 MB free on a 460 GB volume. That is worth recording beside the crash narrative exps 260-262 built on: a disk this full is an independent explanation for a SQLite-backed suite dying at the memory-heavy scenario 15 and for the parent never exiting, and it has never been ruled out. Not asserted here — untested — but it should be checked before the next runner attributes that crash to the peer.
claims.conditions: M1 Pro · macOS 26.2 · host at 0.0% idle and ~400 MB free disk throughout · 2026-08

claims.text: The `select()` isolate round trip is 6.3 us of an 8.4 us canonical 6-column point read. Measured by running the query on the calling isolate instead — same `resqlite_stmt_acquire_on`, same `decodeQuery`, no SendPort and no `Isolate.exit` — which is worth a reproduced -74.8% there, -71.0% on a 21-column point read and -35.7% on a 20-row page. Two collections of four alternating-order lane-isolated AOT passes (41 then 51 samples/lane), `ab_drift_check` REPRODUCED on every primary pair in the second collection; both control lanes return more rows than the cap admits, run byte-identical code in both arms, and read +0.1% and +3.2%. Unlike claim 264.1 the effect is flat in projection width, because what it removes is per-request rather than per-slot. The routing candidate that produced this number is REJECTED (claim 265.6); the number is not, and it is the denominator any future candidate in this direction should be compared against. Collected against 4b963ad, before exp 266's stickiness landed; exp 266's term decays to -1.6% by a statement's eight-thousandth execution and every lane here runs well past that, so the pricing should hold on current main but was not re-measured there.
claims.conditions: M1 Pro · macOS 26.2 · Dart 3.12.2 · AOT CLI bundle · lane-isolated, 4 alternating-order passes x 2 collections · host at 0-39% CPU idle · pre-266 baseline · 2026-08

claims.text: Routing a `select()` to the calling isolate on the strength of a per-SQL row-count high-water mark is REJECTED, because row count cannot bound main-isolate work along three independent axes. (1) Bytes: one row can be arbitrarily large, `SELECT * FROM photos WHERE id = ?` keeps a permanent high-water mark of 1, and with no hop to serialise for, exp 236's 256 KB blob wrap is suppressed — so a 5 MB image copies straight onto the calling isolate, unchecked. Cost varies per execution of the same statement, so no per-SQL history repairs it. (2) Query cost: `count(*)` over a large table and an unindexed `ORDER BY ... LIMIT 10` return few rows after unbounded work, which a result-shape signal cannot see because the work precedes the first row. (3) Scheduling: an inline `select()` returns a `List` rather than a `Future`, so a chain of them drains in microtasks with no event-loop turn — N reads are one uninterruptible block, not N interleavable slices, evidenced by exp 265's own `point1` lane at 200 reads / 427 us. The first draft of the writeup claimed a `~16 us per admitted read` bound; that was the bound for the measured shapes (small integers, short TEXT, indexed lookups, hot cache) stated as though general. Prototype preserved at `archive/exp-265`.
claims.conditions: M1 Pro · AOT · analysis against the exp 265 prototype; failure modes identified by inspection, not measured — the discriminating lanes do not exist yet · 2026-08

claims.text: A read that never enters the dispatch queue is ~19x faster than one that does when the pool is busy. One point read issued while four outstanding 1,000-row reads occupy all four workers measures 533-1169 us across four passes against 37-52 us inline (-94.9% mean, REPRODUCED in both pairs). The hop's cost to a caller is its latency plus the queue depth in front of it, and every prior measurement of transfer cost in this direction held the request population constant and therefore measured only the first term. Independent of exp 265's rejection: it is a property of the queue, not of the routing policy.
claims.conditions: M1 Pro · AOT · `point-under-load` lane, 4 background 1,000-row reads, 10 timed point reads/sample · 2026-08

claims.text: Serialising concurrent point reads on one isolate beats spreading them across the four-worker pool. Eight distinct point reads issued together via `Future.wait` measure -70.3% inline (REPRODUCED, both pairs, 10 groups per sample). The pool's parallelism cannot recover a per-request overhead larger than the request itself, which bounds where the pool is worth having: above the size at which decode dominates dispatch, and not below it.
claims.conditions: M1 Pro · AOT · `concurrent8` lane, 8 distinct 1-row statements x 10 groups/sample · 2026-08

claims.text: An abort-and-fall-back cap costs +24.7% on the one execution that trips it, once per statement, and is the one part of exp 265's design that survives its rejection — because it enforces rather than predicts. A statement armed by two one-row executions and then returning 400 rows starts decoding inline, throws past row 64, resets and re-runs on a worker: 129 us against 163 us, REPRODUCED in both pairs. It cannot recur, because the high-water mark rises with the large result. The reset is not optional: a statement abandoned mid-iteration holds its connection's read transaction open, and every later read on that connection is then served from the pre-abort snapshot. Any future routing design should reuse this shape and add byte and VM-step caps beside it, rather than improving the predictor in front of it.
claims.conditions: M1 Pro · AOT · `cap-abort` lane, fresh SQL string per sample · 2026-08

claims.text: A reader connection reserved for the calling isolate costs +0.1 to +1.7 MB of peak RSS, with two of nine lanes reading slightly down — at or below what exp 261's guard resolves (claim 261.2). Expected, since a connection's page cache is demand-filled and the inline connection reads pages the workers have already made resident. Recorded because it prices the connection for any future design that needs one: it cannot be shared with an idle worker, since the reply that frees a worker slot is sent before the worker's `finally` releases its connection, so `isAvailable` on the main isolate does not imply idle in C, and the connections are `SQLITE_OPEN_NOMUTEX`.
claims.conditions: M1 Pro · AOT · maxRss, one process per lane, 9 lanes · 2026-08

claims.text: Reader-pool dispatch stickiness — starting `ReaderPool._dispatch`'s scan at the slot that served the previous read rather than the next one — is worth a reproduced -32.2% on a statement's first four executions, -21.8% on its first eight and -13.2% on its first thirty-two, decaying to -1.6% by the eight-thousandth. In absolute terms four sequential point reads of a fresh statement fall from 58 us to 39 us, and the saving is dominated by a term paid once per statement rather than by a per-read rate: ~19 us across the first four executions, ~22 us across the first eight, ~30 us across the first thirty-two. The mechanism accounts for the magnitude — round-robin makes all four reader connections prepare the statement, build its schema and warm its pages, so the candidate avoids three cycles of roughly 6-9 us each, and the percentage falls because an increasing execution count is what it is divided by. Twenty-four alternating-order lane-isolated AOT passes in two collections of twelve, 121 samples per lane per arm; all 24 passes were faster on `first4-newsql` and `first8-newsql`, 22 of 24 were faster on `first32-newsql`, and the shipped-code collection classified all 12 `first4`/`first8` pass-pairs plus four of six `first32` pairs as REPRODUCED. The other two `first32` pairs reversed sign across the order flip and were marked drift-suspected by `ab_drift_check.dart`.
claims.conditions: M1 Pro · macOS 26.2 · Dart 3.12.2 · AOT CLI bundle · 4-worker pool · lane-isolated, 24 alternating-order passes, 121 samples/lane · host 71% idle · 2026-08

claims.text: Stickiness costs concurrency nothing, because a busy preferred slot falls through to the next exactly as a round-robin scan did. Over 24 passes, four concurrent reads read +1.3%, eight against a four-worker pool (so dispatch parks on `_dispatchWaiters`) +0.2%, and a 60,000-slot result that crosses `sacrificeSlotThreshold` and ends its worker on every sample -0.4% — each sign-flipping between the two collections (`conc4` is -1.4% in one and +1.5% in the other), which is what marks them neutral rather than small. The property is pinned deterministically rather than through the noisy lanes: `test/reader_pool_test.dart` asserts that four reads issued without awaiting leave `availableWorkerCount` at zero, which fails if stickiness ever queues them on one worker.
claims.conditions: M1 Pro · AOT · `conc4` / `conc8` / `mixed6-10k` lanes, 24 alternating-order passes · 2026-08

claims.text: A fixed per-(statement, worker) cost is structurally invisible to resqlite's benchmark suite, and this is a property of the suite rather than of any one lane. Every release scenario and every focused harness lane executes one statement from tens to thousands of times per sample, because that is what it takes to resolve a per-read effect at microsecond scale; a cost paid once per statement per worker is divided by that repeat count before it is ever reported. The discriminating instrument is a lane that mints a fresh SQL string per sample (a trailing comment leaves the plan identical) and times its first N executions. Three such lanes at N = 4, 8 and 32 bracket where the fixed term stops mattering, and the monotonic decay across them is stronger evidence for a warm-up mechanism than any single lane's magnitude.

Two candidate per-read costs on the reader hop are refuted by direct probe and should not be attempted again without a new mechanism. First, the per-TEXT-cell `Pointer.asTypedList` view allocation in `decodeQuery`: decoding 40,000 24-byte cells through one fresh external view each costs 432 us against 378 us through a persistent window with offsets, so the view is ~1.35 ns/cell, about 1.5% of the 10k x (4 INT + 4 TEXT) read exp 251 measured at 3,587 us — and routing the bytes through a native scratch buffer to earn it would add a copy larger than the saving. Second, the per-query `RowSchema` copy across the isolate hop: an isolate ping-pong carrying a worker-cached schema (names list plus eagerly built HashMap index) against one carrying no schema at all differs by under 1% of a round trip at 6 and 21 columns and at 1, 20 and 1,000 rows — under 40 ns, indistinguishable from noise. Neither is worth an experiment.
claims.conditions: M1 Pro · standalone AOT probes, no SQLite · 2026-08

claims.text: A dispatch-policy change can break a reclaim path that is driven by traffic, and `selectBytes` is the case in this codebase. Exp 183's `json_buf` reclaim shrinks a reader connection's serialization buffer when a later, *smaller* read arrives on that same connection; a concurrent burst of large byte reads grows all four readers' buffers, and only the round-robin rotation brings the settling small reads back round to reclaim them. Making every read sticky left the three workers a burst had grown unvisited, and `Diagnostics.readerJsonBufHighWaterBytes` settled at 6.2 MB against the 512 KB the exp 185 release guard allows — a real retention regression that the wall-time harness could not see and the guard caught on its first run. `selectBytes` therefore keeps the pre-266 rotation while `select` sticks. The boundary is structural rather than expedient: the bytes path retains a per-connection buffer whose reclaim is traffic-driven, and the rows path retains nothing per connection. Pinned by a `selectBytes keeps rotating` unit test and by the `bytes-first8-newsql` harness lane, which reads -1.2% (7 of 12 passes faster) as an unchanged path should.

Sticky reader dispatch does not regress stream fan-out: the stream-rerun-dispatch Tracelite preset (high-cardinality-fanout, keyed-pk-subscriptions, many-streams-writer-throughput) measured -10.7%/-20.5%/-7.5% elapsed against origin/main, none slower, with warmup guardrails all pointing down 36-53% (too noisy to classify individually). The keyed-PK -20.5% at p~1e-5 hints stream reruns themselves benefit from landing on a warm worker, but no stream win is claimed from a guard run.
claims.conditions: Tracelite A/B, stream-rerun-dispatch direction preset, arm64 macOS; harness verdict 'inconclusive' only because the preset gates on a 43.5% improvement expectation

claims.text: Raising the three SQL-keyed read-path caps (`STMT_CACHE_MAX`, `_schemaCacheMax`, `ReaderPool.rowSizeMemoryMax`) from 32 to 128, together with in-place LRU-slot reclaim in `stmt_cache_insert`, is worth a reproduced -55.5% at 40 rotating distinct statements, -55.1% at 64 and -53.3% at 128, on a lane issuing 256 point reads per sample. Per read that is 14.0 us -> 6.1 us. The win is flat across 40-128 statements, which is the cliff signature; every lane inside the old cap (`rotate8`, `rotate24`, `rotate32`, `point1`) is neutral in two independent order-flipped collections, and peak RSS rises 0.8-1.2 MB.
claims.conditions: M1 Pro · macOS 26.2 · Dart 3.12.2 · AOT CLI bundle · 4-worker pool · lane-isolated, 4 alternating-order passes, 51 samples/lane, two independent ab_drift_check pairs · host 62-72% idle · 2026-08

claims.text: The statement cache's eviction compaction cost `(STMT_CACHE_MAX - 1) * ~1.6 KB` of `memmove` per prepare and dominated the capacity question. Raising the cap alone measured a reproduced +42.1% on `churn-unique` (256 never-repeated statements per sample); removing the compaction took the same lane to a reproduced -11.9%, an improvement over the 32-entry baseline. The compaction preserved no ordering that `stmt_cache_lookup_entry`'s promote-by-swap had not already given up.

claims.text: A bounded SQL-keyed cache returning the wrong entry is silent, not fatal: the caller receives a well-formed result belonging to a different statement. `test/stmt_cache_pressure_test.dart` gates this by pushing 400 distinct statements through every cache and checking each statement's identity from its result — the row it selects, the columns it projects, its parameter arity, and a stream's dependency capture after churn. Four of the five tests were verified to fail against a deliberately mismatched entry (a new `sqlite3_stmt` installed under the evicted entry's old SQL text).
claims.conditions: JIT `dart test`, 400 distinct statements against 128-entry caps · 2026-08

claims.text: Removing worker dispatch has a large, reproducible effect on hot small reads. The exact final candidate measured point reads at -60.0% to -64.9%, page20 at -38.2%, page64 at -24.0%, a point read queued behind four busy readers at -89.5%, and eight concurrent point reads at -69.8% over two order-flipped pairs. claims.text: Rows, result payload bytes, VDBE-opcode count and a stopwatch checked before a synchronous call do not bound caller-isolate wall time. After two one-byte arming reads, `SELECT length(randomblob(?))` with a 16 MiB argument returned one INTEGER in 25,975-27,790 us without crossing any proposed cap. A 1 ms timer fired before return on worker-first main in all three samples and failed to fire before return on the inline candidate in all three. The expensive built-in function call occurs inside one VM opcode, so a progress handler cannot preempt it.

claims.text: A SQLite progress handler is a cancellation opportunity, not wall-time preemption. SQLite invokes it at selected VM loop boundaries; one function, collation, virtual-table, VFS/page-fault or busy-handler interval may run before another check. In the rejected prototype, parameter packing and cold statement preparation also occurred before handler installation, reader connections retained a 5-second busy timeout, and native TEXT classification scanned a complete cell before Dart applied the output-byte cap.

claims.text: The 1 ms per-turn budget measures and improves yielding across a chain of cheap reads, not the duration of one read. In the focused final-candidate lane, worst timer lateness was 1,253-1,313 us inline against 2,373-2,382 us through dispatch; making the budget unreachable produced a separate 33,344 us observation. The opaque-work probe shows why this cannot be promoted to a per-read wall bound.

claims.text: Release-suite auto-comparison can silently choose a stale or non-release artifact. Exp 269's first sweep compared against a two-experiment-old anchor and reported four apparent regressions on unreachable paths; an explicit same-host baseline from the actual parent cleared them, yielding 1 win, 0 regressions and 168 neutral metrics. Always name the parent receipt explicitly and test diff reachability before interpreting an aggregate flag.
